name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 15 November 1969

clue.text: Bully the manager overturned in the race?

indicators.note: something overturned is knocked over and upset, so its letters land in a new order
'in' places the reworked letters inside the other piece, which wraps around them

blocks.note: the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man
the seven letters of manager, rearranged

explanation.surface: A tyrannical manager comes a cropper during a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The race' reads as any contest, but it is the Isle of Man TT, whose two letters bracket the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A termagant is a violent, overbearing, scolding person, typically a woman, who browbeats those around her.

clue.text: Sofa where two heads are better than one?

definitions.text: Sofa where two heads are better than one?

blocks.clueFragment: Sofa where two heads are better than one?
blocks.note: surface reading: a piece of furniture that suits a pair, punning on the proverb about two heads
setter's reading: the French name of the S-shaped sofa means head to head, two people facing each other

explanation.surface: A sofa built for a cosy pair, nodding at the proverb that two heads are better than one.
explanation.walkthrough: Tête-à-tête is French for head-to-head; the name is given to an S-shaped two-seater on which the sitters face each other.
explanation.definitionFit: A tete-a-tete is a Victorian double seat shaped so two people sit side by side facing opposite ways for private conversation.

clue.text: "A lovely woman in a --- lovely spot" (! Leigh Hunt)

definitions.text: "A lovely woman in a --- lovely spot" (! Leigh Hunt)
definitions.note: the answer is the word missing from the quotation

blocks.clueFragment: "A lovely woman in a --- lovely spot"
blocks.note: surface reading: a quoted line with a gap where one word has been removed
setter's reading: the line is attributed, with a doubtful exclamation, to Leigh Hunt; the gap wants an adjective for countryside

explanation.surface: A quotation, credited with a wink to Leigh Hunt, about a lovely woman in a lovely place.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing adjective describes a pleasant spot in the countryside. Leigh Hunt was an English Romantic poet and essayist.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing adjective, meaning of the countryside, completes the quoted line about the pretty country place.

clue.text: The chap in the attic?

blocks.note: surface reading: a lodger living in a roof space
setter's reading: Attic means belonging to Attica, the region around Athens, so the chap is a citizen of that city

explanation.surface: A man living up in the loft of a house.
explanation.walkthrough: The lower-case 'attic' hides the proper adjective Attic, of Attica and its capital Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of ancient Athens was an Attic man, Attica being the territory that surrounded the city.

clue.text: Ben's ill-conceived in stone, can you deny it.

indicators.note: something ill-conceived is badly put together, so these letters are assembled wrongly
'in' places the jumbled letters inside the other piece, which wraps around them

blocks.note: agate is a banded semi-precious stone
the letters of Ben, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone challenges you to deny that a man named Ben was badly carved in stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ill-conceived in stone' reads as a botched statue; the closing 'can you deny it' wraps the definition in a challenge.
explanation.definitionFit: To abnegate is to renounce or refuse something, especially to deny oneself a right or comfort.

clue.text: The Shogun's in business

definitions.note: the answer is a person in business, a magnate

blocks.note: first meaning: the title by which foreigners knew the Japanese shogun, meaning great lord
second meaning: a wealthy and powerful industrialist

explanation.surface: The Japanese military ruler has gone into commerce.
explanation.walkthrough: The business sense came from the Japanese title taikun, used for the shogun when dealing with foreigners.
explanation.definitionFit: The word was the Western title for the shogun and now names a rich magnate who dominates an industry.

clue.text: Cattle guide

blocks.note: first meaning: a young castrated bull raised for beef
second meaning: to direct the course of something

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words suggest a drover; they are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A bullock raised for beef is one of the beasts in a herd, and to direct a vehicle's course is to guide it.

clue.text: One bound thither encountered several septets

definitions.text: One bound thither encountered several septets

blocks.clueFragment: One bound thither encountered several septets
blocks.note: surface reading: a traveller who met groups of seven on the road
setter's reading: the nursery riddle in which a traveller meets a man with seven wives, each with seven sacks, each holding seven cats, each with seven kits

explanation.surface: A traveller on the way somewhere met several groups of seven.
explanation.walkthrough: The riddle begins 'As I was going to St Ives, I met a man with seven wives'. St Ives is a town in Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: The narrator of the old nursery riddle is heading for this Cornish town when meeting the man, his wives, sacks, cats and kits.

clue.text: The fourth river of Eden

blocks.note: surface reading: a plain question of Bible knowledge
setter's reading: Genesis lists Pison, Gihon and Hiddekel, then names the last of the four rivers flowing out of Eden

explanation.surface: A Bible quiz question about the rivers of the Garden of Eden.
explanation.walkthrough: Genesis 2:14 ends the list: 'And the fourth river is Euphrates.'
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis names this Mesopotamian waterway as the last of four streams parting from the garden's river.

clue.text: The sort of rhyme to incur ruin?

indicators.note: to ruin something is to wreck it, leaving its letters smashed into another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Asks what kind of verse could bring about disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incur ruin' reads as a phrase, but ruin is an instruction to wreck incur. Poe's The Bells speaks of 'a sort of Runic rhyme'.
explanation.definitionFit: Runic verse is ancient Norse or Germanic poetry, and Poe's poem The Bells uses the phrase for mysterious chanting.

clue.text: Paper for illuminating presumably

definitions.note: read as two words, a lamp switched on

blocks.note: first meaning: a rough-surfaced handmade paper favoured by watercolourists
second meaning, split in two: a flashlight switched on, as you would have it when lighting the way

explanation.surface: A sheet of paper meant for illuminating, as in decorating manuscripts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Illuminating' suggests illuminated manuscripts and so paper; the setter means giving light, as a torch that is on does. Torch is the British word for a flashlight.
explanation.definitionFit: Torchon is a coarse, heavily textured watercolour paper, named from the French for a rough cloth or duster.

clue.text: "These wounds I had on 's day" (Henry V)

definitions.text: "These wounds I had on 's day" (Henry V)
definitions.note: the answer is the word missing from the quotation

blocks.note: surface reading: a soldier's line with a name dropped before the possessive
setter's reading: the King's speech before Agincourt, imagining old veterans rolling up their sleeves to show their scars on the feast day

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Henry V about an old soldier's scars.
explanation.walkthrough: In the speech before Agincourt the King says the veteran will strip his sleeve and show his scars, saying 'These wounds I had on Crispin's day.'
explanation.definitionFit: Agincourt was fought on 25 October, the feast of the shoemaker saints whose name completes the quoted line.

clue.text: Exhausted by one kind of single combat

definitions.note: the answer is a modifier for a style of wrestling

blocks.note: first meaning: utterly tired out
second meaning: a freestyle form of wrestling with few holds barred

explanation.surface: A fighter worn out by a one-on-one duel.
explanation.walkthrough: All-in wrestling is a British term for freestyle professional wrestling, where almost any hold is allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being completely spent is an informal British meaning, and the same phrase names wrestling with nearly no restrictions on holds.

clue.text: Eric got me to be concerned about figures

indicators.note: concerned can mean troubled and agitated, so the letters before it are stirred into another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Eric persuaded me to worry about the numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concerned about figures' reads as one phrase meaning worried over sums; split it, and 'concerned' works on Eric got me while 'about figures' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Geometry is the study of shapes, so anything geometric relates to lines, angles and other plane or solid shapes.

clue.text: Selectors' items

blocks.note: surface reading: things belonging to the people who pick a sports team
setter's reading: passages taken from a book by someone compiling a selection

explanation.surface: The belongings or business of a team's selection panel.
explanation.walkthrough: Selectors suggests cricket or football selectors; the clue means an anthologist choosing passages.
explanation.definitionFit: Passages chosen and copied out of a longer text are the pieces an anthologist picks for a collection.

clue.text: Novice inclines to jolly hat-wearers!

blocks.note: a tyro is a beginner
leans means tilts or inclines

explanation.surface: A beginner warms to cheerful people in hats.
explanation.definitionFit: People from the Austrian Alpine region of Tyrol are known for the green felt hat with a feather, and for yodelling cheer.

clue.text: Male character from the Eve of St Agnes

indicators.note: characters taken from a written title are letters lifted straight out of its words

blocks.note: the first four letters run across both words

explanation.surface: A male figure in Keats's poem The Eve of St Agnes.
explanation.walkthrough: Character suggests a person in the poem; it means the letters of its title.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag is an adult male deer, and the word also means men only, as in a party for the groom.

clue.text: Soppy welcome from Jock

definitions.note: the answer is a Scots participle used as a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: in Scots, to greet is to weep, so greeting is tearful, soppy crying
second meaning: salutations offered on arrival

explanation.surface: A sentimental reception from a Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Jock is a nickname for a Scot, telling you to use the Scots verb greet, meaning cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Salutations given to arriving guests make up a welcome, while the Scots word for weeping supplies the tearful sense.

clue.text: These shoes can tell a tale!

definitions.note: the answer is people who can tell a tale

blocks.note: first meaning: soft rubber-soled shoes that make no noise
second meaning: telltales, people who sneak on others

explanation.surface: Shoes so worn they could tell a story.
explanation.walkthrough: To sneak is British school slang for telling tales to a teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: Quiet rubber-soled plimsolls are named for stealthy walking, and schoolchildren who inform on classmates are also so named.

clue.text: Fairy gets a fish, a bit fruity!

blocks.note: a peri is a fairy in Persian mythology
a carp is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A fairy catches a fish and becomes somewhat saucy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit fruity' sounds like slightly risque; it means a part of a fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The pericarp is the wall of a ripened ovary, the part of a fruit surrounding its seeds.

clue.text: An by right, by courtesy a man" (Austin)

definitions.text: An by right, by courtesy a man" (Austin)
definitions.note: the answer is the word missing from the quotation

blocks.clueFragment: An by right, by courtesy a man"
blocks.note: surface reading: a quoted line with a word dropped after its first word
setter's reading: Alfred Austin, Poet Laureate, contrasting a nobleman's inherited rank with his worth as a man

explanation.surface: A line from Alfred Austin about rank and manhood.
explanation.walkthrough: The completed line reads 'An earl by right, by courtesy a man'. Alfred Austin was Britain's Poet Laureate from 1896.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a British noble title inherited by right, ranking below a marquess and above a viscount.

clue.text: German boot?

blocks.note: surface reading: footwear made in Germany
setter's reading: Boot is German for boat, and the full German word for a submarine lacks only its first part

explanation.surface: A German boot, as in footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The U in U-boat stands for Unterseeboot, undersea boat; the answer is the German word that goes before Boot.
explanation.definitionFit: Untersee means undersea in German, the first half of the word for a submarine before the noun for boat.

clue.text: Implying that brunettes are biased?

definitions.note: the answer is what brunettes are said to be

blocks.note: first meaning: not blonde, i.e. not light-haired
second meaning: not just or even-handed

explanation.surface: A suggestion that dark-haired people are prejudiced.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the word as un-fair: brunettes, being dark-haired, are not fair in the sense of light-coloured.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone partial or prejudiced treats people without justice or equality, and dark-haired people lack light colouring.

clue.text: Rumpus caused by one aspect of atomic explosion?

definitions.note: the answer is the phrase for breaking something apart

blocks.note: first meaning: a noisy quarrel or brawl
second meaning: the splitting of the atom, broken into pieces

explanation.surface: Asks whether a commotion was set off by a nuclear blast.
explanation.walkthrough: Bust-up is British slang for a row; read literally, an atom that splits is busted up.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud fight or quarrel is an informal noun, and smashing something apart is the literal verb phrase.

clue.text: Marigold's vulnerary

definitions.note: here a noun: a remedy for wounds

blocks.note: first meaning: the botanical genus of the pot marigold
second meaning: an ointment made from the flowers and used to heal wounds

explanation.surface: The healing preparation made from a marigold.
explanation.walkthrough: A vulnerary is a medicine for healing wounds, from Latin vulnus, wound.
explanation.definitionFit: Pot marigolds belong to this genus, and their petals make a soothing antiseptic salve still sold under the Latin name.

clue.text: Gold reserve perhaps?

blocks.note: surface reading: a nation's official bullion holdings
setter's reading: a hidden store of anything, gold being just one example

explanation.surface: A central bank's stockpile of bullion.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'perhaps' warns that gold is only one example of what may be kept in the store.
explanation.definitionFit: A cache is a secret hoard of valuables, provisions or weapons hidden away for later use.

clue.text: Short punishment task

blocks.note: surface reading: a brief chore given as a penalty
setter's reading: the answer is a shortened form of a longer word for a school penalty

explanation.surface: A quick chore handed out as a punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools an imposition was lines or extra work set as a punishment; pupils shortened the word.
explanation.definitionFit: School slang clipped imposition, the written exercise a teacher sets as a penalty, to this short form.

clue.text: Matthew gets a First in poetry

blocks.note: first meaning: the English poet and diplomat Matthew ...
second meaning: earlier, preceding

explanation.surface: A student named Matthew earns a first-class degree in poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: A First is a top-class British university degree; here it means coming before. 'In poetry' points to the poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthew Prior wrote light verse around 1700, and the surname as an adjective means earlier or preceding.

clue.text: Paradoxically like the silent American?

blocks.note: surface reading: a contradictory description of a quiet person from the United States
setter's reading: Americans clam up, so the word reads as clam-like, yet it really means noisy

explanation.surface: A puzzling description of a taciturn American.
explanation.walkthrough: Clam up is American slang for falling silent, so the word looks as if it means clam-like; the paradox is that it means the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Clamant comes from Latin clamare, to cry out, and means loudly insistent or noisy, the reverse of silent.

clue.text: Lion ate in a state of high spirits

indicators.note: to be in a state is to be agitated and flustered, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lion feeds while in a cheerful mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A state of high spirits' reads as the definition, but 'in a state' is the instruction and only 'high spirits' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Elation is great happiness and exhilaration, the feeling of being on top of the world.

clue.text: Expressionist artist in censorious mood

indicators.note: 'in' says the name sits inside the following word, enclosed by its other letters

blocks.note: letters two to six of the word

explanation.surface: A painter in a fault-finding frame of mind.
explanation.definitionFit: James Ensor was a Belgian painter whose masks and grotesque crowds made him a forerunner of Expressionism.

clue.text: Essential travel books

blocks.note: surface reading: guidebooks one must read before a trip
setter's reading: small bound documents without which you cannot cross a border

explanation.surface: A reading list of must-have guides for travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: Travel books suggests guides or memoirs; the books meant are the little booklets checked at frontiers.
explanation.definitionFit: These official booklets prove identity and nationality and are required for international journeys.
